title: Titles, labels and units
summary: A chart without words is a puzzle. Every chart needs a title that says what it shows (or, better, what it found), and labels on both axes with their units. A title can even be worked out from the data, so it stays true for any file.
objectives: Add a title and axis labels with plt.title(), plt.xlabel() and plt.ylabel().
Write a headline title that says what the chart found.
Work out a headline from the data with idxmax().

slides.h: By the end: a chart that explains itself
slides.say: Show the rain bars to someone with no title and no labels: “rain of what, in what?” Three short lines answer it before they ask.
points: `plt.xlabel("Month")` across the bottom; `plt.ylabel("Rain (mm)")` up the side.
Units in brackets: mm, °C, people, ₹ lakh.

slides.say: A label title says what the chart **is**: “Rain by month”. A headline says what it **found**: “July is the wettest month”. Readers remember headlines.
points: Label title: fine for a reference chart.
Headline: when the chart makes a point.
The headline must be true for the data drawn.

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
df = pd.read_csv("weather.csv")
wet = df.loc[df["Rain_mm"].idxmax()]
plt.bar(df["Month"], df["Rain_mm"])
plt.title(f"{wet['Month']} is the wettest month")
plt.ylabel("Rain (mm)")
